title: Vignette
description: A vignette in vignette cinematography darkens, desaturates, or lowers contrast toward the frame edges because of optical falloff, mechanical vignetting in the barrel, a filter, or a later grade. Optical vignette follows the lens, while a post oval is a drawing.

sections.title: Narrative function

blocks.text: The corners lose stop. Attention pools in the center without a spotlight on the actor.
Vintage wide glass and some anamorphics do this unasked. Cameo lighting can look similar, but that is a lighting plot, not falloff in the optic.
Use it to hold the eye in, to mimic old glass, or to admit that the field is darker off axis. Keep it gentle enough that the sides still exist.

It is the wrong tool as a heavy post oval crushed onto every wide. If the edges go to black like a spotlight and the falloff is a perfect geometric shape unrelated to the lens, you have a filter, not an optic.

sections.title: How it works

blocks.text: Wide-open vintage glass, a wide angle on a small coverage circle, or an ND or grad at the edges. Cosine-fourth falloff is natural.
Mechanical vignetting is the barrel cutting the bundle. In a grade, darken corners with a soft, lens-shaped roll, not a hard oval.
Prompt: natural optical vignette, edges falling off, vintage falloff, not a post oval.

sections.title: When to use it

blocks.text: A rooftop figure at blue hour, corners a stop down, center holding the coat and the city. Do not crush the sides of a group shot until the people at the edge disappear.

sections.title: In film

blocks.text: Barry Lyndon shows fast vintage glass with natural corner falloff in candlelit rooms. The Witch uses older optics whose edges go quietly, holding the eye in the clearing or the kitchen.

sections.title: What usually goes wrong

blocks.text: Wrong cousin: a circular crop, cameo spotlight, or a heavy social-media oval. Tell: perfect ellipse of black, subjects at the edge crushed, no relation to the lens.
Fix: soft, stop-based roll, keep edge information, match the glass.

sections.title: Questions

blocks.text: What is a vignette in film?
Darkening or contrast loss at the frame edges from optics, the barrel, a filter, or a grade. Optical vignette is falloff. A post oval is an added shape.
Vignette vs cameo lighting
Cameo lighting is a dark set with a figure lit in the middle. A vignette is the frame itself losing light toward the corners, even if the set is even.
When should I use a vignette?
To hold the eye in or to match vintage glass. Do not crush the sides as a default filter, especially on groups and wides that need the edges.
How do I prompt a vignette for AI image or video?
Request natural optical falloff, a stop or so in the corners, and no hard post oval. Name vintage glass if that is the cause.
